## The frame of a block: layer normalization and residual connections {#sec-te-block}

This section covers steps 7, 18, 19 and 20 of the Explainer's tour.

Before we look inside the attention layer and the MLP, look at how they are connected, because the Explainer draws the connections only as faint lines and dots, and they matter. Write $X$ for the $n \times 768$ matrix that enters a block. The block computes

$$
\begin{aligned}
X &\leftarrow X + \operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{LN}(X)), \\
X &\leftarrow X + \operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{LN}(X)),
\end{aligned}
$$

where the arrow means that the matrix on the right replaces $X$. So each part receives a normalized copy of $X$, computes something of the same shape $n \times 768$, and that is added to $X$. @fig-te-residual draws it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-residual
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The frame of a transformer block, as in @fig-te-overview. A copy of the stream is normalized (LN), the attention layer or the MLP computes a change of the same shape, and the change is added back to the stream at the plus. The lanes that run straight past the part are the residual connection."
residual()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| column: margin
overview(detail=1)
```

The addition is called a *residual connection*, and the Explainer marks it with the lines labeled Residual. Because of it, neither part replaces a token's list of numbers. Each only has to work out what to add, and everything that was in $X$ before flows past it unchanged. You can think of $X$ as a running record for each token that the twelve blocks write into, one addition at a time. This is also why every part must return a matrix of exactly the shape it received: otherwise the addition would not be defined. Residual connections were invented to make deep networks trainable ([He et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR.2016.90)). In [Backpropagation](../neural_networks/training.qmd#sec-train-backprop) you saw that the gradient reaches a weight by being multiplied through every layer between it and the loss. Through an addition, the gradient passes unchanged, so even the first block of a deep stack receives a usable signal.

The second piece of the frame is *layer normalization*, written LN, which the Explainer draws as small dots before each part and once more before the output. It works on each token's list of 768 numbers separately. For one list $x = (x_1, \dots, x_{768})$, it computes the mean and the standard deviation of the numbers,

$$
\mu = \frac{1}{768} \sum_{i=1}^{768} x_i, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{768} \sum_{i=1}^{768} (x_i - \mu)^2},
$$

and then

$$
\operatorname{LN}(x)_i = \gamma_i \, \frac{x_i - \mu}{\sigma} + \beta_i .
$$

Subtracting $\mu$ and dividing by $\sigma$ makes the 768 numbers have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, whatever they were before. Then each number is stretched by its own learned weight $\gamma_i$ and shifted by its own learned bias $\beta_i$. (GPT-2 adds a tiny number, 0.00001, to $\sigma^2$ before taking the square root, so that it never divides by zero.) Take the list $(2, 4, 4, 6)$ as a small example. Its mean is 4, its variance is $(4 + 0 + 0 + 4)/4 = 2$, so $\sigma = \sqrt 2 \approx 1.41$, and the normalized list is $(-1.41, 0, 0, 1.41)$. Layer normalization is not a layer of neurons in the sense of @fig-te-dense, because every output depends on all the inputs through $\mu$ and $\sigma$, which are not weighted sums with fixed weights. The learned part is only the 768 values of $\gamma$ and the 768 values of $\beta$. What it does for the network is keep the numbers in a range where the layers that follow work well, however large the additions from the earlier blocks have made them.

The last step of the tour shows *dropout*, which only matters during training. While GPT-2 was trained, a random tenth of the numbers at a few places in each block were set to 0 at every step, so that the network could not come to rely on any single number. When the trained model is used, as in the Explainer, dropout is switched off and does nothing.

#### Exercise

[SOLO](../intro/course-introduction.qmd#sec-badge-solo){.small}

Work these out on paper, with $\gamma_i = 1$ and $\beta_i = 0$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Normalize the list $(1, 3, 5, 7)$.

The mean is 4. The squared differences from the mean are 9, 1, 1 and 9, so the variance is $20/4 = 5$ and $\sigma = \sqrt 5 \approx 2.24$. The normalized list is $(-3, -1, 1, 3)/2.24 \approx (-1.34, -0.45, 0.45, 1.34)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Now normalize $(10, 30, 50, 70)$, which is ten times the list above. What do you notice, and why does it happen?

The mean is 40 and $\sigma = \sqrt{500} \approx 22.4$, and the normalized list is again $(-1.34, -0.45, 0.45, 1.34)$. Multiplying a list by 10 multiplies both $x_i - \mu$ and $\sigma$ by 10, and the two cancel. Layer normalization keeps the pattern of a list and throws away its overall size and its average level, so the parts of the block never see how large the numbers in $X$ have grown.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Why must the attention layer and the MLP each return a matrix of shape $11 \times 768$?

Because their output is added to $X$, which is $11 \times 768$, and two matrices can only be added number by number if they have the same shape.
:::

<br>

## Looking back at the sentence: attention {#sec-te-attention}

This section covers steps 8 to 12 of the Explainer's tour.

To predict what follows "makes copies of its", the model has to know whose copies they are. The word "its" refers to something earlier in the sentence, and the list of numbers for "its" must somehow take in information from the word it refers to. This is what the attention layer does, and it is the only layer in GPT-2 where the tokens of the sentence exchange information. In the Explainer, it is the large panel in the middle of the block. In this section, write $\tilde X = \operatorname{LN}(X)$ for the normalized $11 \times 768$ matrix that the attention layer receives.

### Queries, keys and values

Attention starts by computing three new matrices from $\tilde X$, called the *queries*, the *keys* and the *values*:

$$
Q = \tilde X W_Q + b_Q, \qquad K = \tilde X W_K + b_K, \qquad V = \tilde X W_V + b_V .
$$

Each of $W_Q$, $W_K$ and $W_V$ is a $768 \times 768$ matrix, so each of these is a fully connected layer of 768 neurons, applied to every token separately with the same weights in the way of @fig-te-rows. Each result is again $11 \times 768$, and its row $i$ is the query $q_i$, the key $k_i$ or the value $v_i$ of token $i$. In GPT-2's code the three layers are stored side by side as one $768 \times 2{,}304$ matrix, which is the same thing. @fig-te-qkv draws them, as matrices and as neurons, and in the Explainer they are the blue, red and green bands labeled Q, K and V that leave every token.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-qkv
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The query, key and value layers, the left part of the attention in @fig-te-overview. Left: the normalized matrix $\\tilde X$ goes through three fully connected layers, $W_Q$, $W_K$ and $W_V$, applied to every token with the same weights, and each result is cut into 12 blocks of 64 columns, one per head. Right: the same three layers for one token, drawn as neurons, with 4 inputs and 3 neurons per layer instead of 768."
qkv_layers()
```


```{python}
#| echo: false
#| column: margin
overview(detail=2)
```

The three play different parts. The query of a token says what the token is looking for. For "its", a useful query would be something like "a noun earlier in the sentence that could own something". Nobody writes this down in words. The query is a list of numbers, and what the numbers stand for is whatever turned out to be useful in training, but it helps to think of it as a question the token asks about the tokens before it. The key of a token says what it has to offer to anyone who is looking: what kind of token it is and what part it plays in the sentence. The key of "virus" might stand for something like "a noun, a living thing, the one doing something in this sentence". The value is what a token hands over when another token pays attention to it. It is a separate list from the key because what makes a token easy to find is not the same as what is useful to receive. To be found by "its", it helps "virus" to be a noun that can own things. What "its" needs to receive is what kind of thing a virus is, because that decides whether the next word is "DNA", "genes" or something else entirely.

### Twelve heads

A single set of queries, keys and values can only look for one thing at a time. So the 768 columns of $Q$, $K$ and $V$ are divided into 12 blocks of 64 columns each, called *heads*:

$$
Q = \begin{bmatrix} Q_1 & Q_2 & \cdots & Q_{12} \end{bmatrix},
$$

and the same for $K$ and $V$. Head $h$ works only with $Q_h$, $K_h$ and $V_h$, each of shape $11 \times 64$. In terms of neurons, each of the three layers of 768 neurons is simply divided into 12 groups of 64, and each group is used by one head. The heads do the same calculation side by side, each with its own weights, and each can learn to look for something different. In the Explainer, the Head 1 of 12 arrows at the bottom of the attention panel step through them. Everything that follows happens in one head, and we drop the subscript $h$ for a moment.

### From scores to attention weights

To decide how much attention token $i$ should pay to token $j$, the model compares the query of $i$ with the key of $j$ by their dot product $q_i \cdot k_j = q_{i1}k_{j1} + \dots + q_{i,64}k_{j,64}$. The dot product is large when the two lists have large numbers with the same sign in the same places, that is, when what one token is looking for matches what the other has to offer. Every query must be compared with every key, and all those dot products at once are one matrix product:

$$
S = \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{64}} .
$$

$K^\top$ is $K$ *transposed*: its rows written as columns, so it has shape $64 \times 11$. The product of the $11 \times 64$ matrix $Q$ with the $64 \times 11$ matrix $K^\top$ is $11 \times 11$, and its entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $Q$ with column $j$ of $K^\top$, which is $q_i \cdot k_j$. So $S$ is a square table of scores with one row and one column per token. The division by $\sqrt{64} = 8$ keeps the scores from growing with the length of the lists. If the 64 numbers in $q$ and $k$ are of size around 1, their dot product is a sum of 64 products, and a sum of 64 independent terms of size around 1 typically lands some $\sqrt{64} = 8$ away from zero. Dividing by 8 brings the scores back to a size around 1.

Two more steps turn the scores into weights. First comes the *mask*. Every score for a token after token $i$ is set to minus infinity, by adding the matrix

$$
M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } j \le i, \\ -\infty & \text{if } j > i. \end{cases}
$$

This means that a token can only look back at itself and the tokens before it, never ahead. That is a must for a model that is trained to predict the next token: if it could look ahead, it would just read the answer. Then each row goes through *softmax*:

$$
A_{ij} = \frac{e^{S_{ij} + M_{ij}}}{\sum_{k} e^{S_{ik} + M_{ik}}} .
$$

Raising $e$ to the power of each score makes every number positive and makes high scores much higher than low ones, and dividing by the row's total makes the numbers in each row add up to 1. A score of minus infinity becomes $e^{-\infty} = 0$. The result $A$ is the attention table in @fig-te-attention, with one row per token saying how its attention is divided among the tokens up to and including itself. When you zoom in on the purple grid in the Explainer, it shows these three stages, the dot products, the scaling and mask, and the softmax, as separate grids.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-attention
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Attention weights $A$ in two of GPT-2's 144 attention heads. Each row is a token, and the cells show how much attention it pays to each earlier token. Every row adds up to 1, and the empty upper-right triangle is the mask. The row of \"its\" is outlined and its weights are written in. Left: block 1, head 1, where the attention of \"its\" is spread out. Right: block 5, head 4, where \"its\" pays almost all its attention to the two candidates for owning the copies, \"virus\" and \"cell\"."
attention_tables()
```

### Mixing the values

The new list of numbers for token $i$ is the values of all the tokens, mixed in proportion to the weights in row $i$ of $A$:

$$
z_i = \sum_{j} A_{ij}\, v_j, \qquad \text{or for all tokens at once,} \qquad Z = A V .
$$

$A$ is $11 \times 11$ and $V$ is $11 \times 64$, so $Z$ is $11 \times 64$, one new list of 64 numbers per token. If the weight of "its" on "virus" is large, the new list for "its" is made largely of the value of "virus". @fig-te-head follows one head through the calculation, from its block of columns in $Q$, $K$ and $V$ to its block of columns in $Z$.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-head
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "One attention head, the purple card in @fig-te-overview, here head 4 of block 5. Only head 4's 64 columns of $Q$, $K$ and $V$ are used, and the rest are dimmed. $Q_4$ and $K_4$ give the scores, which scaling, the mask and softmax turn into the attention weights $A$. $A$ times $V_4$ fills the same block of columns in $Z$, where the outputs of the 12 heads sit side by side."
one_head()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| column: margin
overview(detail=3)
```

Each of the 12 heads produces such a $Z_h$. They are put side by side into one $11 \times 768$ matrix and passed through one more fully connected layer, with a $768 \times 768$ matrix $W_O$:

$$
\operatorname{Attn}(\tilde X) = \begin{bmatrix} Z_1 & Z_2 & \cdots & Z_{12} \end{bmatrix} W_O + b_O .
$$

The result has the shape $11 \times 768$, as the residual connection requires, and in the Explainer it is what flows out of the attention panel at Out.

A small example shows how the query, the key and the value work together. Suppose the lists have only two numbers each, and only three tokens come before "its": "virus", "cell" and "makes". The query of "its" is $q = (1, 1)$, and the keys and values of the three tokens are the rows of the matrices in @tbl-te-qkv. To keep the arithmetic simple, we skip the division by 8 and the mask.

| Token | Key | Score $q \cdot k$ | Weight after softmax | Value |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| virus | $(2, 1)$ | $1 \times 2 + 1 \times 1 = 3$ | 0.72 | $(4, 0)$ |
| cell | $(1, 1)$ | $1 \times 1 + 1 \times 1 = 2$ | 0.27 | $(0, 4)$ |
| makes | $(0, -1)$ | $1 \times 0 + 1 \times (-1) = -1$ | 0.01 | $(2, 2)$ |

: A worked example of attention with lists of two numbers. The query of "its" is $q = (1, 1)$. Its dot product with each key gives a score, softmax turns the scores into weights, and the weights say how much of each value goes into the new list for "its". {#tbl-te-qkv}

In matrix form, the scores are $qK^\top = (3, 2, -1)$. Softmax gives $e^3 = 20.1$, $e^2 = 7.4$ and $e^{-1} = 0.37$, which add up to 27.8, so the weights are $20.1/27.8 = 0.72$, $7.4/27.8 = 0.27$ and $0.37/27.8 = 0.01$. The key of "virus" matches the query best, so it gets the highest weight. The new list for "its" is $aV = 0.72 \times (4, 0) + 0.27 \times (0, 4) + 0.01 \times (2, 2)$, which is about $(2.91, 1.09)$. It is made mostly of what "virus" had to offer, partly of what "cell" had, and almost nothing of "makes". This is the same pattern you will find in block 5, head 4 of the real model.

#### Exercise

[SOLO](../intro/course-introduction.qmd#sec-badge-solo){.small}

Use the keys and values from @tbl-te-qkv, change the query of "its", and work out the new weights. You will need a calculator for the softmax.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Change the query to $(0, 2)$. Which token gets most attention now, and what is the new list for "its"?

The scores are $0 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 = 2$ for "virus", $2$ for "cell" and $-2$ for "makes", so "virus" and "cell" tie with weights of about 0.50 each, and "makes" gets about 0.01. The new list is about $(2.00, 2.00)$, an even mix of the two values. This query only looks at the second number in each key, and there "virus" and "cell" are the same, so the head can no longer tell them apart.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Change the query to $(2, 2)$. What happens to the weights, compared with the query $(1, 1)$?

The scores double to $6$, $4$ and $-2$, and the weights become about 0.88, 0.12 and 0.00. The order is the same, but the winner takes more. Multiplying all the scores by a number larger than 1 sharpens the softmax, and dividing them makes it flatter. This is why the real model divides the scores by 8: without it, long lists with many numbers give large scores, and softmax would put almost all the weight on a single token. You will meet the same effect again as the temperature in [From numbers to the next word](#sec-te-output).
:::

<br>

### Attention as a layer of neurons

Now compare attention with the layers in [Layers of neurons are matrices](#sec-te-matrices). Every other layer in GPT-2 has the form $XW$, with the weight matrix on the right. Multiplying on the right combines the numbers within each row, so it mixes the 768 numbers of a token and never mixes tokens. The attention output $Z = AV$ has its matrix on the left. Multiplying on the left combines whole rows, so $z_i$ is a weighted sum of the rows $v_j$ of the other tokens. That is the only place in the model where tokens are combined. Drawn as neurons, as in @fig-te-attention-lines, $A$ is a fully connected layer from the tokens' values to the tokens' new lists, with each line's thickness showing its weight, and with the lines to later tokens removed by the mask.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-attention-lines
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The attention of \"its\" in block 5, head 4, drawn as connections into a neuron, with the tokens in the same order as in the other figures. Each token's value (green) is connected to the new list for \"its\" (magenta), and the thickness of each line is its attention weight, so the new list is made mostly from the value of \"virus\" and partly from that of \"cell\". Unlike the weights in a fully connected layer, these weights are computed from the sentence itself and change when the sentence changes."
attention_lines()
```

The difference from an ordinary layer is where the weights come from. In a fully connected layer, the weights are learned during training and stay the same regardless of the input text. In attention, the weights $A$ are computed afresh from the queries and keys of the text actually present. Feed the model a different sentence, and the same head draws different lines. Training sets the weights $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ and $W_O$, so a head learns how to decide where to look, then applies that to whatever text it is given. This also makes attention the one place in the model where inputs are multiplied with each other: $S$ is a product of $Q$ and $K$, both computed from $\tilde X$, so the weights of the lines depend on the input, and the result $AV$ is again a product of two things computed from $\tilde X$.

Splitting the work into query, key and value is what makes attention useful, for three reasons. The first is that looking and being found are kept apart. If each token had a single list that it used both to look for others and to be found by them, the scores would be dot products of a list with lists like it, and a token would match best with tokens like itself, because the dot product of a list with itself is large. A pronoun does not need other pronouns, though. With separate matrices $W_Q$ and $W_K$, "its" can look for something quite unlike itself. The second is that being found and handing something over are kept apart, too. A head can find a token by one property, such as being a noun, and pass on another, such as what the noun means. The third is that the queries and keys are computed from the text itself, so the connections follow the sentence. "virus" could be two tokens back or two thousand, and the same weights will find it.

This last point is a large part of why the transformer ([Vaswani et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)) replaced the language networks that came before it. Those read text one word at a time and had to carry everything they might need later in a running summary, where information from far back faded. With attention, every token can reach every earlier token directly, and the scores for all pairs are one matrix product, computed at the same time, which suits the graphics chips that AI runs on and made it possible to train much larger models. It also explains something you see when you use an assistant. Everything in the conversation, such as the code you pasted or a requirement from your first message, is within reach of every new token through attention, and that is how the assistant can use it. But the weights in a row of $A$ always add up to 1, so in a very long conversation they are shared among many more tokens, and a detail far back can get so little weight that it is overlooked.

With twelve heads in each of the twelve blocks, GPT-2 has 144 heads in all, and nobody told any of them what to look for. Some learn something we can name, such as linking a pronoun to the word it refers to. Many do not. @fig-te-heads shows, for every head in the model, how much attention "its" pays to "virus". Most heads pay little, and a few pay a lot. On average, about half of the attention across all heads goes to the first token, "The". Heads seem to use the first token as a place to park their attention when they aren't looking for anything in particular ([Xiao et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453)). Since each row of $A$ must add up to 1, a head that has nothing to look for has to put its weight somewhere.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-heads
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "How much attention \"its\" pays to \"virus\" in each of the 144 heads of GPT-2, one row per block and one column per head. Weights above 0.2 are written in. Block 5, head 4, which is outlined, pays the most."
all_heads()
```

#### Exercise

[SOLO](../intro/course-introduction.qmd#sec-badge-solo){.small}

Zoom in on the attention part of the first transformer block. The Explainer starts in block 1, head 1, and shows the attention table as a grid of purple cells. Hovering over a cell shows its weight. Zooming in further shows the dot products, the scaling and mask, and the softmax as separate grids.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Why is the upper-right half of the attention table empty?

That is the mask. A cell above the diagonal would be the attention a token pays to a token that comes after it, and the mask sets those scores to minus infinity, which softmax turns into $e^{-\infty} = 0$. A token can only look back.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## What is the weight in the top-left cell, and why must it be exactly that?

1.00. The first token, "The", has no earlier tokens, so every other score in its row is minus infinity. Softmax then gives $e^{S_{11}} / e^{S_{11}} = 1$, whatever the score $S_{11}$ was.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## In block 1, head 1, which token does "its" pay the most attention to?

"The", with a weight of about 0.21, followed by "virus" with about 0.16. In this head, the attention of "its" is spread across the whole sentence.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Move to block 5 and click through the heads to head 4. How much attention does "its" pay to "virus" now, and which token gets most of the rest?

About 0.63 goes to "virus", and about 0.34 to "cell". Together they get almost all of it. This head has learned to send a pronoun's attention to the nouns it might refer to, and here it has two candidates. It favors the virus, which is correct.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Write down the shapes of $Q$, $Q_h$, $K_h^\top$, $S$, $A$, $Z_h$ and $\begin{bmatrix} Z_1 & \cdots & Z_{12} \end{bmatrix}$ for our sentence.

$Q$ is $11 \times 768$, $Q_h$ is $11 \times 64$, $K_h^\top$ is $64 \times 11$, $S$ and $A$ are $11 \times 11$, $Z_h$ is $11 \times 64$, and the twelve $Z_h$ side by side are $11 \times 768$. Note that $S$ and $A$ grow with the square of the number of tokens. For a text of 1,000 tokens, each head computes a table of a million weights, which is why long texts are expensive.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## How many parameters, weights and biases, does one attention layer have?

$W_Q$, $W_K$ and $W_V$ have $768 \times 768 = 589{,}824$ weights each, and each has 768 biases, so together they have $3 \times 590{,}592 = 1{,}771{,}776$ parameters. $W_O$ and $b_O$ add another $590{,}592$, for $2{,}362{,}368$ in all. The attention weights $A$ are not parameters. They are computed from the text every time.
:::

<br>

## The MLP {#sec-te-mlp}

This section covers step 13 of the Explainer's tour.

After the attention layer, each token's list goes through a small network of two fully connected layers, which the Explainer calls the *MLP*, short for multi-layer perceptron. With $\tilde X = \operatorname{LN}(X)$ again the normalized $11 \times 768$ matrix, it computes

$$
\operatorname{MLP}(\tilde X) = \operatorname{GELU}(\tilde X W_1 + b_1)\, W_2 + b_2 .
$$

$W_1$ is $768 \times 3{,}072$, so the first layer has 3,072 neurons, four times as many as there are inputs, and $\tilde X W_1 + b_1$ is $11 \times 3{,}072$. GELU is an activation function applied to each of these numbers separately, as in [Activation functions](../neural_networks/neurons.qmd#sec-nn-activation). $W_2$ is $3{,}072 \times 768$ and brings each list back to 768 numbers, so the result is $11 \times 768$ as the residual connection requires. Both matrices are on the right, so the MLP applies to each token independently, using the same weights for every token, as @fig-te-mlp shows. It is the one-token-wide convolution from [Layers of neurons are matrices](#sec-te-matrices). In the Explainer, it is the light blue band that widens and narrows again, and hovering over it shows the sizes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-mlp
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The MLP, the teal part of @fig-te-overview. Left: $W_1$ widens each token's stripe to 3,072 numbers, GELU is applied to each number, and $W_2$ brings each stripe back to 768. Right: the same network for one token, drawn as neurons with 3 inputs, 6 hidden neurons and 3 outputs instead of 768, 3,072 and 768. The same weights are used for every token, and no line connects one token to another."
mlp()
```


```{python}
#| echo: false
#| column: margin
overview(detail=4)
```

GELU is a smooth relative of the [ReLU](../neural_networks/neurons.qmd#sec-nn-relu) you have met before. It is defined as $\operatorname{GELU}(x) = x\,\Phi(x)$, where $\Phi(x)$ is the probability that a number drawn from a standard normal distribution is smaller than $x$. For large positive $x$, $\Phi(x)$ is almost 1 and GELU passes $x$ through, and for large negative $x$, $\Phi(x)$ is almost 0 and GELU gives 0, just like ReLU. In between, it bends smoothly instead of at a sharp corner, and it dips slightly below zero, as @fig-te-gelu shows. GPT-2 computes it with the approximation

$$
\operatorname{GELU}(x) \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\, x \left(1 + \tanh\!\Big(\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\big(x + 0.044715\, x^3\big)\Big)\right).
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-gelu
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "GELU, the activation function in GPT-2's MLP, next to ReLU. Both pass large positive numbers through and turn large negative numbers into 0. GELU bends smoothly and dips slightly below zero for small negative numbers."
gelu()
```

Nobody fully understands what the MLPs do, but they hold most of the model's weights, and studies of them suggest that much of what a model has picked up about the world, such as which words go with which facts, is stored there ([Geva et al., 2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.446/)). One way to read the equation supports this. Each of the 3,072 hidden neurons computes a dot product of the token's list with its column of $W_1$, so it responds to a particular pattern in the list. When it responds, GELU lets its output through, and the neuron adds its row of $W_2$ to the result, scaled by how strongly it responded. So the MLP is a set of 3,072 pattern detectors, each of which writes its own list of 768 numbers into the token's record when its pattern is present.

#### Exercise

[SOLO](../intro/course-introduction.qmd#sec-badge-solo){.small}

Zoom in on the MLP in the first block, and hover over its parts to see their sizes.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## How many numbers does the middle column hold for each token, and how does that compare with the columns on either side?

The middle column is a vector of 3,072 numbers, and the side columns are vectors of 768. The MLP first expands each token's list to four times its length and then shrinks it back.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Does any line in the MLP go from one token to another? Answer from the equation as well as from the screen.

No. Every token goes through the MLP on its own. In the equation, both $W_1$ and $W_2$ multiply from the right, which mixes numbers within each row but never combines rows. The only place in the block where tokens take in information from each other is $AV$ in the attention layer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## How many parameters does one MLP have, and what is GELU of 0, of 3 and of $-3$, using the approximation in the text?

$W_1$ and $b_1$ have $768 \times 3{,}072 + 3{,}072 = 2{,}362{,}368$ parameters, and $W_2$ and $b_2$ have $3{,}072 \times 768 + 768 = 2{,}360{,}064$, so one MLP has $4{,}722{,}432$. GELU(0) is exactly 0. For 3, the expression inside the tanh is $0.798 \times (3 + 1.21) \approx 3.36$, and $\tanh(3.36) \approx 0.998$, so GELU(3) $\approx 0.5 \times 3 \times 1.998 \approx 3.00$. For $-3$, the tanh is about $-0.998$, so GELU($-3$) $\approx 0.5 \times (-3) \times 0.002 \approx -0.004$, almost 0.
:::

<br>

## Twelve blocks {#sec-te-stack}

This section covers step 7 of the Explainer's tour.

A block takes an $11 \times 768$ matrix and returns one of the same shape, so the blocks can be chained, and GPT-2 chains twelve of them. They are built the same way, but each has its own $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, $W_O$, $W_1$, $W_2$, biases and layer normalization parameters. The Explainer draws only the first and writes "11 more identical Transformer Blocks" behind it. You can move between them with the arrows next to Transformer Block 1.

So the list of numbers for each token runs through twelve blocks and is refined at each step by two additions. You can get a rough idea of how the prediction forms by taking the list for the last token after each block and sending it straight to the [output layer](#sec-te-output), as if the model ended there. @fig-te-lens shows the result. Up to block 9, the model's best guess is "own", which is a sensible continuation of "makes copies of its" when you only know the grammar. Only in blocks 10 to 12 does "DNA" take over, once the information about the virus has been worked in. The early guesses should be taken with a grain of salt, because the output layer was trained only to read the list after the last block, but the picture of a guess gradually reshaped from block to block is borne out by many such experiments. It is also what the residual connections lead you to expect: each block adds to the record instead of rewriting it, so the record after block 9 is still most of the record after block 12.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-lens
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The probability of \"own\" and of \"DNA\" as the next token if the model stopped after each of its twelve blocks and sent the last token's numbers straight to the output layer. The model settles on \"DNA\" only in the last three blocks."
lens()
```

#### Exercise

[SOLO](../intro/course-introduction.qmd#sec-badge-solo){.small}

You now know every matrix in GPT-2. Use the parameter counts from the earlier exercises to answer these on paper.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## How many parameters does one transformer block have?

The two layer normalizations have $2 \times (768 + 768) = 3{,}072$ parameters, the attention layer $2{,}362{,}368$ and the MLP $4{,}722{,}432$, which makes $7{,}087{,}872$ per block. Two thirds of them are in the MLP.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## GPT-2 is said to have 124,439,808 parameters. Can you account for all of them?

Twelve blocks have $12 \times 7{,}087{,}872 = 85{,}054{,}464$. The token embedding $E$ adds $50{,}257 \times 768 = 38{,}597{,}376$, the position embedding $P$ adds $1{,}024 \times 768 = 786{,}432$, and the final layer normalization before the output adds $1{,}536$. The total is $124{,}439{,}808$. The output layer adds nothing, because it reuses $E$, as you will see in the next section.
:::

<br>

## From numbers to the next word {#sec-te-output}

This section covers steps 14 to 17 of the Explainer's tour.

After the twelfth block, only the last row of $X$ is used, the $1 \times 768$ list $x_{11}$ for "its", because only the last token has seen the whole sentence. It is normalized once more and sent through one last fully connected layer, with 50,257 neurons, one for each token in the vocabulary:

$$
z = \operatorname{LN}(x_{11})\, E^\top .
$$

$E^\top$ is the embedding matrix transposed, of shape $768 \times 50{,}257$, so $z$ is $1 \times 50{,}257$. GPT-2 reuses the [embedding matrix](#sec-te-embedding) for the weights of this layer, so the score of token $t$ is the dot product of the normalized list for "its" with the embedding of $t$. A token gets a high score when the list points in the same direction as its embedding. The scores are called *logits*, and when you zoom in on Probabilities, the Explainer lists them in the column Logits. @fig-te-output shows the whole path from the last block to the probabilities.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-output
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The output, the right end of @fig-te-overview. After the last block the stream is normalized, and only the stripe of \"its\" is multiplied by $E^\\top$, the transposed embedding matrix, which gives one logit for each of the 50,257 tokens. Dividing by the temperature, keeping the top k, and softmax turn the logits into probabilities."
output()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| column: margin
overview(detail=5)
```

Softmax turns the logits into probabilities, the same function the attention layer uses. Before softmax, the logits are divided by a number $T$ called the *temperature*:

$$
p_t = \frac{e^{z_t / T}}{\sum_{s} e^{z_s / T}} .
$$

A temperature below 1 makes the differences between the logits larger, so the most likely token becomes even more likely. A temperature above 1 makes the differences smaller and evens out the probabilities. It is the same effect you saw when you doubled the query in the exercise with @tbl-te-qkv, and the division by 8 in attention is a fixed temperature of 8. The Explainer shows $z/T$ in the column Scaled logits. @fig-te-temperature shows the effect on the bars.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-temperature
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The five most likely next tokens at three temperatures, computed the way the Transformer Explainer computes them with its default top-k of 5, where only the five most likely tokens are kept, and their probabilities are rescaled to add up to 1. A low temperature makes \"DNA\" almost certain. A high one evens the five out."
temperature()
```

Last comes the choice. The model could always take the most likely token, which is called *greedy* decoding, but that produces dull, repetitive text, so assistants usually *sample*: they draw a token at random, with each token's chance of being drawn equal to its probability. Two settings limit the draw to the likely tokens. *Top-k* keeps only the $k$ most likely tokens, and *top-p* keeps the most likely tokens until their probabilities add up to at least $p$. Both are done the way the attention mask is: the logits of the tokens that are thrown away are set to minus infinity before softmax, so they get probability 0, and the probabilities of the kept tokens automatically add up to 1. The Explainer shows the result in the column Top-k, where the discarded tokens read $-\infty$, and it starts with top-k and $k = 5$. To save time, it also looks only at the 50 highest logits before doing any of this, and treats the other 50,207 tokens as if they were impossible. At the default temperature, those tokens together have only about 2% probability, so the bars change very little, but top-p can differ slightly from GPT-2 without the shortcut. The answers below are computed the Explainer's way.

When a token is drawn, it is added to the end of the text, and the whole calculation runs again on the longer text, now with $n = 12$, to choose the next token. You can do this by hand in the Explainer: clicking into the text box adds the drawn token to the end of your sentence, and Generate runs the model again on the longer text. An assistant does the same thing automatically, which is how it writes its reply one token at a time.

#### Exercise

[SOLO](../intro/course-introduction.qmd#sec-badge-solo){.small}

Zoom in on Probabilities on the right of the Explainer. The temperature slider and the top-k and top-p settings are above it. Before you move a slider, decide what you think will happen to the probability of "DNA", and then move it to check.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## At the default settings, temperature 0.8 and top-k with k = 5, what are the probabilities of "DNA" and of "genes"?

"DNA" is about 73.3% and "genes" is about 11.1%. The other three are "own", "genome", and "genetic", with about 5.6%, 5.4%, and 4.6%.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Read the logits of "DNA" and "genes" in the Logits column. Compute $e^{(z_{\text{DNA}} - z_{\text{genes}})/0.8}$ and compare it with the ratio of their two probabilities. Why do they agree?

The logits are about $-107.91$ and $-109.43$, a difference of $1.52$. Then $e^{1.52/0.8} = e^{1.90} \approx 6.7$, and the ratio of the probabilities is $73.3/11.1 \approx 6.6$, the same up to rounding. In the softmax formula, both probabilities have the same denominator, which cancels when you divide one by the other, leaving $e^{z_{\text{DNA}}/T} / e^{z_{\text{genes}}/T} = e^{(z_{\text{DNA}} - z_{\text{genes}})/T}$. Only the differences between logits matter. That is also why it does no harm that all the logits are large negative numbers: adding the same number to every logit changes nothing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Set the temperature to 0.2. What is the probability of "DNA" now? And at 2.0?

At 0.2, "DNA" gets about 99.9%, and the model will practically always choose it. At 2.0, it drops to about 39.8%, and even "genetic", the least likely of the five, gets about 13.2%.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Set the temperature back to 0.8 and switch from top-k to top-p. The Explainer starts top-p at p = 0.5. How many tokens have a probability above zero?

Only one: "DNA", with 100%. "DNA" alone already has more than half the probability, so top-p with p = 0.5 stops after the first token, and Generate can only choose "DNA".
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## Now set p to 0.9. How many tokens are left, and which one is new compared with the five that top-k kept?

Six tokens: "DNA", "genes", "own", "genome", "genetic", and "cells". "cells" is new, with about 4.4%. "DNA" drops to about 70.1% because its probability is now shared with one more token.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal" icon=false}

## With the default settings, about how often would you expect the model to choose a word other than "DNA"?

About 27% of the time, a little more than one time in four, because "DNA" has a probability of about 73%. The same model with the same settings and the same sentence will therefore often write something else. That is why an assistant gives you a different answer when you ask the same question twice.
:::

## The whole model on one page {#sec-te-summary}

Put together, everything GPT-2 does to choose the next token fits in a few lines. For a text of $n$ tokens with one-hot rows $O$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
X &= O E + P_{0:n} && n \times 768 \\
\text{in each of the 12 blocks:} \quad X &\leftarrow X + \operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{LN}(X)) && n \times 768 \\
X &\leftarrow X + \operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{LN}(X)) && n \times 768 \\
z &= \operatorname{LN}(x_n)\, E^\top && 1 \times 50{,}257 \\
p &= \operatorname{softmax}(z / T) && 1 \times 50{,}257
\end{aligned}
$$

with, for the normalized input $\tilde X$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Attn}(\tilde X) &= \begin{bmatrix} Z_1 & \cdots & Z_{12} \end{bmatrix} W_O + b_O, \qquad Z_h = \operatorname{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{Q_h K_h^\top}{8} + M\Big)\, V_h, \\
\operatorname{MLP}(\tilde X) &= \operatorname{GELU}(\tilde X W_1 + b_1)\, W_2 + b_2,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $Q = \tilde X W_Q + b_Q$, $K = \tilde X W_K + b_K$ and $V = \tilde X W_V + b_V$ are split into twelve heads of 64 columns each. Every line is a matrix product, an addition, or a function applied to each number or each row. All of it is layers of neurons with weighted sums, except for the two places where something else happens: $Q_h K_h^\top$ and the product with $V_h$, where two matrices computed from the text are multiplied with each other, and layer normalization, where each list is rescaled by its own mean and standard deviation. The 124 million parameters are the numbers in $E$, $P$, the $W$s, the $b$s, and the $\gamma$s and $\beta$s, all set by the gradient descent you met in [Walking downhill](../neural_networks/training.qmd#sec-train-descent), on the single task of making the observed next token in a large amount of text as probable as possible.

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-overview-final
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The whole of GPT-2 again, as in @fig-te-overview. Every element is one of the lines in the equations above."
overview()
```

## What you have seen {#sec-te-explains}

Everything an AI assistant does is built on the steps you just followed, but in a much larger model. Text is cut into tokens based on how often pieces of text occur, so the model sees chunks of letters, not single letters. Each token becomes a row of a learned embedding matrix, with related words ending up close together. Twelve blocks of attention and fully connected layers then add to those rows. In GPT-2, the fully connected layers multiply from the right and so treat each token independently, using the same weights for all of them, and attention, which multiplies from the left, is the only place where tokens take in information from each other. It computes its weights afresh for each new text. At the end, the model gives a probability for every token in its vocabulary, and a token is drawn at random from the most likely ones.

Several things you will notice about assistants follow directly from this. An assistant can give a different answer to the same question because it draws the next token at random. It can state something false with complete fluency because it chooses a token that is likely given the text, and nothing in the calculation checks it against the world. In our sentence, "genes" and "cells" were never far behind "DNA", and in a different sentence the wrong word can just as easily be the likely one. It has no memory between messages, because all it ever sees is the text in front of it. When an assistant seems to remember what you said earlier in a chat, it is because the whole conversation is sent to it again as one long text. And it is hard to predict what a particular weight or head does, because nobody chose any of them. You saw one head that links a pronoun to its noun, and 143 others that do things nobody has named.

GPT-2 was large for its time, but it's small now. Today's assistants have more blocks, wider layers, more heads, and can read far longer texts at once, and they are trained on much more data, with further training to help them answer questions. But they are built from the same parts you have seen here, and they still work one token at a time.
